authors: Perkins DM, Yvon-Durocher G, Demars BOL, Reiss J, Pichler DE, Friberg N, Trimmer M, Woodward G
title: Consistent temperature dependence of respiration across ecosystems contrasting in thermal history
n_sites_or_obs: 13 streams (2 days each within 11 days, August 2008)
method: OLS of ln(daily whole-stream ER) on 1/kT - 1/kTc (Tc = 15 C) across streams; two-station open-system O2 method with lateral-inflow correction; RQ 0.85
notes: Published value for the same whole-stream data as Demars et al. 2011 (KMAE); supersedes the round-1 computed row Demars2011KMAE ER 0.68 (0.17-1.18), which it matches. r2 = 0.44. Single summer survey: across-stream (space-for-time) estimate; ER not partitioned.

authors: Perkins DM, Yvon-Durocher G, Demars BOL, Reiss J, Pichler DE, Friberg N, Trimmer M, Woodward G
title: Consistent temperature dependence of respiration across ecosystems contrasting in thermal history
n_sites_or_obs: 4 streams x 3 opaque benthic chambers (3-h in situ incubations)
method: Linear mixed-effects model (lme4), ln(R) vs centred 1/kT, random intercept by stream; Winkler O2 in bottomless dark chambers
notes: In-situ benthic respiration across the thermal gradient; indistinguishable from whole-stream value and from 0.65.

authors: Perkins DM, Yvon-Durocher G, Demars BOL, Reiss J, Pichler DE, Friberg N, Trimmer M, Woodward G
title: Consistent temperature dependence of respiration across ecosystems contrasting in thermal history
n_sites_or_obs: 4 donor streams x 4 replicate biofilms x 6 temperatures (91 of 96 units retained)
method: Acute laboratory incubations (30 min per temperature, ascending sequence); lmer with common slope across streams
notes: Short-term (acute) thermal response, coded experimental_warming as for Padfield 2017. Stream-specific E 0.44-0.51, not different among streams despite natal temperatures 6-25 C and high species turnover; common Q10 1.9 (1.7-2.0). Cubic and quadratic terms did not improve fits, so no curvature (no decline in Q10) up to 30 C. Intercepts (R at 15 C) tracked biofilm biomass (r = 0.98), not stream temperature.

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis
region: geothermal streams in North America (17), Iceland (48) and Kamchatka (4)
n_sites_or_obs: 69 sites (50 measured here + 19 published hot-spring values at 33-70 C)
method: Nonlinear least squares of ln(GPP) to the Johnson-Lewin model (Sharpe-Schoolfield without low-temperature inactivation), Tc = 35 C; enthalpy of activation 52.0 kJ/mol converted as Ea = dH + RT
notes: Supersedes round-1 abstract-only row. 68% CI 0.41-0.72. TEMPERATURE OPTIMUM of whole-ecosystem GPP = 45 C (68% CI 33-57; 95% CI 21-70). Johnson-Lewin preferred over full Sharpe-Schoolfield (AIC 181.4 vs 184.7). Summer, clear, shallow, unshaded groundwater-fed streams; authors report temperature unrelated to light, hydrology and (inconsistently) chemistry. ER was not given an Ea in geothermal streams because ER was constrained by GPP (Suppl. Fig. 1.3).

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis
region: Iceland (4 geothermal areas: Hengill, Hveragerdi, Torfajokull, Vonarskard)
method: Linear mixed-effects Arrhenius model (lme4), random slope and intercept by geothermal area, Tc = 20 C; open-channel diel O2
notes: Nested natural experiment within independent geothermal areas; area-specific slopes did not differ (chi2 = 2.7, P = 0.26). Conditional R2 0.74, marginal 0.38. Authors compare with mass-specific GPP 0.3-0.5 eV in heated channels (Welter et al. 2015).

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis
region: global synthesis (Japan 23, Europe 51, America 110, Africa 10, New Zealand 28 reaches)
method: Linear regression of ln(GPP) on standardised 1/kT across reaches; whole-stream open-channel estimates only, site values averaged
notes: +/- is s.e.m. Across-site, summer only; R2 = 0.18. Authors attribute the high value partly to stream size (light).

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis
region: global synthesis (Japan, Europe, America, Africa, New Zealand)
method: Linear regression of ln(ER) on standardised 1/kT across reaches
notes: +/- is s.e.m.; R2 = 0.13. ln GPP and ln ER correlated (R2 = 0.46). NEP was unrelated to temperature (R2 = 0.0006, P = 0.71) and to discharge, although ER exceeded GPP.

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis
method: Multiple regression of ln(GPP) on 1/kT plus stream discharge (no interaction)
notes: Discharge-adjusted (proxy for stream size and light); model R2 = 0.26. Authors: closer to their prediction (~0.6 +/- 0.15).

authors: Demars BOL, Gislason GM, Olafsson JS, Manson JR, Friberg N, Hood JM, Thompson JJD, Freitag TE
title: Impact of warming on CO2 emissions from streams countered by aquatic photosynthesis

notes: Discharge-adjusted ER.

authors: Jankowski K, Schindler DE, Lisi PJ
title: Temperature sensitivity of community respiration rates in streams is associated with watershed geomorphic features
n_sites_or_obs: 11 streams; 91 chamber incubations (2 per temperature x 5 temperatures per stream)
method: 4-h dark-chamber incubations of streambed gravel in water baths; linear mixed model ln(CR) vs 1/kT - 1/kTc (Tc = 20 C), random intercepts for stream and water bath
notes: Acute benthic community respiration (includes algal respiration), July-Aug 2011; coded experimental_warming as for other acute curves. Q10(5-15 C) 2.7. Stream-specific E digitised here from Fig. 2B (approximate): about 0.38-1.36 eV, median about 0.75 (11 streams); E rose with DOC (R2 0.46) and C:N (R2 0.58) and fell with watershed slope (R2 0.32). Not the same study as JankowskiSchindler2019 (in-situ diel).

authors: Jankowski K, Schindler DE, Lisi PJ
title: Temperature sensitivity of community respiration rates in streams is associated with watershed geomorphic features
method: As above, with DOC concentration and C:N as covariates (best models)
location_in_paper: Results p.2710 (Appendix E Table E1 not seen)
notes: Q10(5-15 C) 2.9. Conditional on DOC and C:N; do not pool with the 0.70 row.

authors: Jankowski K, Schindler DE, Lisi PJ
title: Temperature sensitivity of community respiration rates in streams is associated with watershed geomorphic features
region: USA (Wood River basin, SW Alaska; 51 streams)
n_sites_or_obs: 51 streams (11 measured + 40 predicted from watershed slope)
method: Basin-scale unweighted mean of stream E, 40 streams predicted from the E-watershed slope regression (Monte Carlo)
notes: Modelled upscaling, not a direct measurement. Discharge-weighted 0.82 (SE 0.06); DOC-load-weighted 0.84 (SE 0.08, 15 streams); Q10 3.3-3.4. Higher than the 11-stream mean because flat, peat-rich watersheds dominate the basin.

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C
title: Increased resource use efficiency amplifies positive response of aquatic primary production to experimental warming
region: Iceland (Hengill; experimental stream IS7 warmed ~3.3 C, reference OH2)
n_sites_or_obs: 1 stream; 20 monthly means (2 years, before and during warming)
method: OLS of ln(areal NPP) on 1/kTc - 1/kT (Tc = 6 C), temperature only (Model 1); NPP = 0.5 x GPP, so slope equals that of GPP; two-station open-channel O2, Bayesian model with light saturation
notes: Whole-stream warming (BACI). Temperature variation is seasonal plus treatment, not light-standardised; R2 0.26. Driven by rises in autotroph biomass (+35%, Ulva bloom) and N supply/use efficiency (DIN use efficiency +289%). Best model (light, DIN uptake, temperature x DIN interaction): apparent Ea 4.89 eV at 1st-quartile DIN uptake and 0.99 eV at 3rd quartile (Results 5.5).

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C
title: Increased resource use efficiency amplifies positive response of aquatic primary production to experimental warming
method: As Model 1 plus light (Table 2 Model 2)
notes: Light-adjusted; not significant. Adding DIN uptake (Model 3) gives 1.0 (-0.6 to 2.6).

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C
title: Increased resource use efficiency amplifies positive response of aquatic primary production to experimental warming

notes: Biomass-specific NPP (0.5 x GPP / autotroph biomass). Light-adjusted (Model 2): 0.9 (-1.2 to 3.0). Best interaction model: 4.40 eV at low and 0.32 eV at high DIN uptake. Biomass Eb ~0.49-0.67 eV.

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C
title: Increased resource use efficiency amplifies positive response of aquatic primary production to experimental warming

method: COMPUTED HERE: BACI contrast [ln(During/Before) experimental - ln(During/Before) reference] / [1/k(279.15 K) - 1/k(281.75 K)], using Table 1 means and the reported 2.6 C mean temperature anomaly
notes: Not a published estimate. Table 1 means are rounded to 0.1 g C (GPP 0.4 -> 1.1 experimental; 0.6 -> 0.6 reference), so precision is low. Using the full 3.3 C warming instead of the 2.6 C anomaly gives 2.08 eV. GPP increase significant (pRIA 0.049).

authors: Hood JM, Benstead JP, Cross WF, Huryn AD, Johnson PW, Gislason GM, Junker JR, Nelson D, Olafsson JS, Tran C
title: Increased resource use efficiency amplifies positive response of aquatic primary production to experimental warming
n_sites_or_obs: 2 streams; annual means of monthly rates before vs during warming
method: COMPUTED HERE: same BACI contrast for ER (0.9 -> 1.6 experimental; 1.8 -> 2.0 reference, g C m-2 d-1)
notes: Not a published estimate; ER change not significant (pRIA 0.263). With 3.3 C: 0.97 eV. ER and GPP rose by the same absolute amount (0.7 g C m-2 d-1), so NEP was unchanged; in relative terms GPP rose more than ER.

authors: Kraemer BM, Chandra S, Dell AI, Dix M, Kuusisto E, Livingstone DM, Schladow SG, Silow E, Sitoki LM, Tamatamah R, McIntyre PB
title: Global patterns in lake ecosystem responses to warming based on the temperature dependence of metabolism
region: global (64 metabolism-linked variables applied to 271 lakes)
method: Median of Boltzmann-Arrhenius Ea values compiled from published data (Dell et al. 2013 database and others), fitted below the temperature of maximum performance
notes: Not a primary estimate. Quartiles 0.41-0.80 (not a CI); mean 0.63; range 0.019-1.55. Ecosystem primary production variables 0.30-0.45 eV and ER 0.55-0.63 eV (benthic 0.55, pelagic 0.63) are borrowed from Yvon-Durocher et al. 2010 and 2012 (already in round 1): do not double count. Kraemer label 0.41 eV as planktonic GPP from Yvon-Durocher 2010, whereas round 1 records 0.41 as NPP and 0.45 as GPP in that paper. No lake GPP or ER rates reported.

authors: Lopez-Urrutia A, San Martin E, Harris RP, Irigoien X
title: Scaling the metabolic balance of the oceans
region: global ocean (paired production and respiration data set)
n_sites_or_obs: almost 1,000 paired GPP and community respiration measurements
method: Slope of ln(GPP/CR) vs 1/kT (reported +0.36 eV against 1/kT; sign set negative here as for Bernhardt2022 GPP/ER row)
notes: GPP/CR ratio falls with temperature; the slope estimates E_R - E_P = 0.36 eV (95% CI 0.30-0.42) against the predicted 0.33. Temperature taken from World Ocean Atlas where not reported (42% of pairs). No separate community-level GPP or CR Ea is given in the paper. Threshold GPP for balance rises from <1 mmol O2 m-3 d-1 in cold water to >4 above 15 C (Fig. 4C); 0.4 mmol O2 m-3 d-1 for AMT cruises.
